title: Appendix A: Recovery Instrumentation and Auditing

sections.title: Auditing Both Sides of an External Effect

html:
A payment authorization can time out while the provider continues processing it. A notification consumer can finish reading an event while the email it created is still waiting to be sent. A recovery worker can make twenty status requests without learning whether the original operation succeeded. In each case, the application may be running normally while an accepted obligation remains unfinished.

During an incident, engineers need to know which operations still require attention, how long they have been waiting, and whether recovery is making progress. They also need evidence that the application’s records agree with the systems where external effects occurred. A healthy worker process and a rising attempt counter cannot answer those questions on their own.

This appendix develops the measurements and audits used by Baodium’s recovery workers. The same approach applies to document processing, account provisioning, reservations, external API calls, and any workflow that can continue after the request that started it.

Measuring Unfinished Work

Suppose a recovery queue contains ten operations created a minute ago and another that has been waiting for three hours. A queue-depth measurement of eleven is accurate, but the three-hour operation deserves attention even if the next recovery pass resolves the other ten.

Baodium reported four measurements for each recovery category.

Outstanding work.

The number of distinct operations with an unresolved obligation. Retrying the same operation increases its attempt count without increasing the number of business operations.

Oldest unresolved age.

The time since the earliest unresolved obligation was created. Another attempt, a new worker lease, or transfer to manual review does not reset its original timestamp.

Arrival and resolution rates.

The rate at which obligations enter the category and the rate at which they reach a recorded final outcome. Moving an operation from automatic recovery to manual review is a transfer, recorded separately from resolution.

Attempt outcomes.

The results of individual recovery attempts, including established external outcomes, temporary errors, inconclusive observations, and cases requiring review.

Each category needs a documented starting event and completion condition. An outbox publication obligation begins when the transaction creates its outbox record. A payment-reconciliation obligation begins when the payment outcome becomes uncertain. A compensation obligation begins when the application records that a previous external effect needs corrective action.

Those clocks should survive changes in workflow state. If an unresolved payment is transferred to manual review after two hours, the review has a new assignment timestamp while the underlying payment retains its original unresolved age. Otherwise, moving work between queues can make an old obligation appear recent.

Backlog depth and age also need throughput context. If unresolved work is arriving at twelve tasks per minute and workers complete ten, the backlog grows by two each minute. Adding workers is useful only if they can increase completed outcomes without exceeding the limits of the dependency being investigated. Chapter 12 showed why increasing Kafka consumers did not help Baodium when the notification provider was already at its permitted rate.

Collecting a Consistent Measurement Snapshot

The recovery exporter read outstanding counts and ages from the operation repository. Its snapshot included every configured category, even one with no outstanding operations. An empty category reported a count and oldest age of zero. An unavailable category or failed database query could not be reported as zero.

The repository used one database snapshot where practical and computed age against the database’s observation time. That avoided calculating a three-hour age by subtracting timestamps from machines whose clocks might differ. The collection queries were indexed and bounded so the exporter could still complete while the backlog was large.

The exporter then published one immutable result for the metrics collector to read. Listing Listing shows the simplified refresh and collection path.

The repository, counter, and metric-emission functions are illustrative. The important part is that a scrape reads one published snapshot rather than observing several gauges halfway through an update. The snapshot must contain the complete expected category set, with each value calculated from the same observation where the underlying store supports that consistency.

If the database read fails, the previous snapshot remains available and the failure counter increases. The collector does not invent a new successful observation. The timestamp records when the database snapshot was taken, which may be earlier than the moment its metrics were scraped.

An alert evaluator checks that observation age before using the counts and ages. For example, an outstanding count of zero from a snapshot taken forty minutes ago does not establish that recovery is current. Comparing its timestamp with the evaluator’s clock also requires an allowance for clock skew. Exporter availability and missing-series checks are separate, because a stopped exporter cannot report its own failure.

The exporter uses bounded labels such as region and recovery category. Operation IDs, payment references, and customer identifiers belong in access-controlled records and diagnostic events. Putting one operation ID in a metric label would create another time series for every operation.

Arrival and resolution rates can be exported as counters or derived from durable state transitions. A counter incremented outside the business transaction can be lost if the process crashes, or incremented again after a retry. Exact business totals therefore come from committed transition records. Runtime counters remain useful for identifying changes in processing rate when their collection limits are understood.

Evidence for One Operation

An engineer who opens an unresolved payment needs a record of what the application intended, what it attempted, and what later observations established. Baodium kept the durable business operation separate from its network attempts.

The operation record contained its stable identity, validated parameters or fingerprint, current business state, state version, creation time, and next permitted action. Where an external provider was involved, it also contained the provider account, operation type, idempotency key, and any external operation identifier that had been returned.

Each attempt recorded whether dispatch had been requested, which identity was submitted, when the caller stopped waiting, and what response it actually received. Later status lookups recorded their own observations. A timeout was an observation about the local wait. The provider could have accepted the authorization before the caller stopped waiting.

That is why dispatch intent was recorded before the network call. If the process terminated immediately afterward, recovery could still find the operation and investigate whether the provider had received it. A missing provider-generated identifier did not justify excluding the operation from recovery, since that identifier might have been returned in the response the caller lost.

The history also recorded when the obligation was last examined, which worker owned the current lease, and whether a result needed manual review. Leases and attempt counters helped coordinate workers, while the business operation identity continued to identify the original customer intent.

Retention was set against the longest applicable recovery, provider idempotency, replay, and audit requirements. Expiring a cached HTTP response did not justify deleting the durable operation history that a later retry might need.

Auditing Both Sides of an External Effect

Recovery workers usually begin with operations the application has already classified as unfinished. An audit can discover a different problem: a local record that incorrectly says the operation is complete, or an external effect for which the application has no corresponding record.

Baodium compared records in both directions. Starting from its own payment operations, the auditor retrieved the corresponding provider results. It also examined the provider’s account-level reports and looked for results that had no matching local operation.

An export service has the same requirement. Checking whether every locally recorded completed export exists in object storage finds missing files. Enumerating objects under the approved storage scope can also reveal an untracked file. Both sides need a stable identifier and an agreed account, tenant, or time interval.

Each audit run recorded its coverage: source account or region, identifiers used for matching, the interval or provider cursor examined, the report version, and the time at which the external source considered that interval complete. It also recorded the mapping between local and external outcomes.

Those outcome mappings deserve attention. A Kafka event acknowledged by a broker is not evidence that a notification was sent. A payment provider’s AUTHORIZED result may correspond to a local checkout that is still pending inventory allocation. The auditor compares the facts each system is responsible for recording rather than requiring their status strings to match.

Late Reports and Coverage Gaps

Provider reports can arrive after the transactions they describe. An audit that checks an interval too early may find no provider record for an operation that later appears in the report. Baodium distinguished a complete, authoritative report from one that was still being assembled.

The auditor revisited overlapping intervals and deduplicated observations using stable operation and report identifiers. Pagination and provider cursors were preserved so a large account could be checked in bounded batches. An incomplete page, failed lookup, or unavailable report produced an evidence-coverage issue. It did not establish that the missing operation had failed.

The discrepancy categories were specific enough to guide investigation: unmatched local operation, unmatched provider effect, conflicting business attributes, conflicting outcome, and unavailable evidence. Cases recorded the source references needed for review without copying unnecessary payment or customer details into operational dashboards.

Checkpointing the Audit

For each batch, the auditor committed its observations and discrepancy cases before advancing the durable checkpoint. A crash after that commit could cause the batch to run again. Stable discrepancy identities and unique constraints prevented the second pass from opening duplicate cases.

A checkpoint was advanced only for the scope and report interval that had actually been examined. It could not move past a missing provider page or an incomplete report as though the interval had been audited. If a previously resolved case developed a new disagreement, the auditor reopened it or recorded a linked occurrence under the approved case policy.

The audit dashboard reported both discrepancies and coverage. A zero mismatch count is useful only when the relevant accounts and reporting intervals were actually examined.

Applying Recovery Evidence Safely

Once a worker obtains provider evidence, it still has to apply that observation to the current local operation. Another worker may have resolved the payment in the meantime, or the customer may have canceled the checkout while reconciliation was running.

Baodium used guarded state changes. An observation was associated with its original operation, and a write checked the expected version and current permitted state. Listing Listing illustrates recording a provider authorization against an attempt whose result was still unknown.

The provider response must first be verified against the original account, operation type, and idempotency identity. The SQL then prevents a stale worker from silently replacing another recorded outcome. If it changes no row, the worker rereads the current record and checks what was already applied. It cannot infer that the provider action failed or that another worker completed the same transition.

Recording authorization also does not automatically authorize order confirmation. If the customer canceled the purchase or inventory can no longer be allocated, the workflow may need a void, refund, or manual review. Those operations receive their own durable identities and recovery records. The external authorization fact and the next permitted business action must both be retained.

An external NOT_FOUND result requires similar care. Its meaning depends on which provider account and operation key were queried, how long the provider retains records, and whether an earlier in-flight call could still complete. When that contract cannot establish definitive absence, the outcome is unresolved. Another lookup, an idempotent retry, or manual review follows the provider’s documented recovery rules.

These are the guarded-transition and operation-identity requirements from Chapter 3. Chapter 12 adds the corresponding transaction and replay rules when recovery is driven by messages. Instrumentation supplies the evidence the worker needs, while the workflow continues enforcing the business rules that decide the next action.

Alerts and Operator Actions

A recovery alert is useful when it identifies a condition an owner can investigate or change. A growing unresolved age might indicate a provider outage, repeated inconclusive lookups, a worker that has stopped advancing, or a case waiting for human review. Increasing queue depth alone cannot distinguish them.

Thresholds came from the customer commitment, expected resolution rate, and the external provider’s recovery window. A payment approaching the end of the provider’s idempotency or status-lookup period might require immediate review even if the backlog contained only that one operation. Conversely, a large backlog of recently created tasks might be acceptable when its measured drain rate met the completion objective.

Baodium’s operational view gave the engineer the last valid measurement time, outstanding count, oldest age, recent arrival and resolution rates, attempt outcomes, and responsible service owner. An alert linked to the underlying protected operation records and the applicable recovery runbook.

The first investigation established whether the measurements were current. The next established where work had stopped progressing and whether the external evidence was complete. Only then could the engineer increase worker capacity, change admission, investigate a provider result, or escalate a case. Adding retries before establishing the previous attempt’s outcome could create another external effect without resolving the first.

The objective of these measurements is straightforward. At any moment, the team should be able to identify which accepted obligations are still unfinished, what the application knows about them, and which action is safe to perform next.
